title: InfoQ Cloud and DevOps Trends Report - 2026
gist: InfoQ's 2026 Cloud and DevOps trends panel places enterprise AI platforms/AI gateways, FinOps-for-AI (tokenomics) and sovereign cloud in the Innovators bucket, promotes AI agents for cloud engineering to Early Adopters, and moves platform engineering and MCP to Early Majority. The sharpest signals: token spend cannot yet be tied to outcomes by any FinOps tool, a six-month AWS regional outage plus the US-East failure pushed reliability back into Late Majority prominence, and half of one European consultancy's regulated clients are migrating back on-prem.

themes.theme: Hub-and-spoke AI platforms replace per-team model wiring

insights.claim: Enterprises are shifting from individual AI coding assistants to centrally governed internal AI platforms built on a hub-spoke model: a centralized AI gateway, an approved model catalog of permitted models, and provisioned team workspaces as spokes.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: API management vendors (Apigee, Azure API Management) inherit the AI-governance chokepoint by extending an existing product line — a low-cost adjacency with high strategic value.
insights.quote: It's a hub-spoke model where you have your centralized AI gateway, so it's basically your API management you talked about, but then for your AI.
insights.locator: Enterprise AI Platforms and AI Gateways

insights.claim: The AI-platform pattern is being driven by three distinct motives — model routing for cost control, in-house hosting for sovereignty, and a governed catalog so a hundred teams do not each make their own model decision.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Model routing for cost control means enterprise demand is model-agnostic by design — bad for any single model vendor's pricing power at the enterprise tier.
insights.quote: model routing for cost control, in-house hosting for sovereignty, and a governed catalog so that a hundred teams do not each make their own model decisions
insights.locator: These platforms remain early

insights.claim: Enterprise AI platforms are still classified as Innovators-stage on InfoQ's adoption graph, with how the hub-spoke model fans out in practice described as an open question.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Pre-chasm status means revenue here is still experimental budget, not committed line items — discount vendor claims of enterprise AI platform traction.
insights.locator: These platforms remain early

insights.claim: No FinOps tool currently on the market can relate per-developer token spend across models back to business outcomes, even though the tools can itemize exactly how many dollars each engineer consumed per model.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: The measurement gap is the single biggest unmonetized opening in FinOps tooling — first vendor to credibly link token spend to outcomes wins the category.
insights.quote: The FinOps tools can tell you that Matt Saunders spent X, Y, Z dollars on tokens in Opus, in Fable, in Sonnet, et cetera. But none of them that I know of can actually relate that back to outcomes.
insights.locator: FinOps for AI and Tokenomics

insights.claim: AI costs are frequently a proxy for something else, which makes them structurally harder to optimize than deterministic cloud line items like storage class or data transfer.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Classic FinOps playbooks do not transfer to AI spend; assume slower savings realization and longer sales cycles for AI cost tooling.
insights.locator: Renato Losio pointed out that AI costs

insights.claim: It remains unresolved whether today's model prices are subsidized to drive lock-in or reflect true long-term cost, which is an unpriced risk sitting under every enterprise AI budget forecast.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A latent margin shock: if inference pricing is subsidized, enterprise AI TCO models and the ROI case for AI-heavy workflows reprice sharply upward.
insights.quote: whether today's model prices are subsidized to drive lock-in, or reflect the real long-term cost
insights.locator: There is also a deeper uncertainty

insights.claim: Agent sprawl is now considered a bigger chaos problem than the microservices era, with waste having shifted from big models and MLOps investments to a long tail of many small agents that existing optimization tooling does not capture.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: Cost leakage is moving from a few large line items to thousands of small ones — favoring observability/attribution vendors over rate-negotiation-style FinOps.
insights.quote: Agents' chaos at the moment is bigger than the Microservices times we saw. We have already hit the big rocks of wastage around AI and cloud optimizations. But now we have smaller opportunities and challenges in the form of agents- so many agents.
insights.locator: Shweta Vohra framed the shape of the problem

insights.claim: The FinOps Foundation has forked out a Tokenomics Foundation, and the Agentic AI Foundation was born under the Linux Foundation, formalizing AI cost and agent governance as standalone standards bodies.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: Foundation formation is the reliable leading indicator that a category is about to standardize and commoditize — track which vendors get seats.
insights.quote: That's why the FinOps Foundation has also forked out the Tokenomics Foundation. At the same time, the Agentic AI Foundation was born under the Linux Foundation.
insights.locator: Shweta Vohra framed the shape of the problem

themes.theme: Sovereignty collides with an American-built estate

insights.claim: Full digital sovereignty is impractical for European enterprises whose entire estate — applications, systems, hyperscalers, down to the core policy system — is American, since becoming sovereign would require rebuilding and re-engineering nearly everything.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Sovereignty demand is real but conversion to migration is slow — expect long sales cycles and partial (IaaS-only) sovereign wins rather than full-stack displacement.
insights.locator: Sovereign Cloud Strategies

insights.claim: European providers can supply IaaS and storage, but the platform and SaaS layers have no obvious sovereign equivalent — a CRM such as Salesforce being the canonical example of an unsubstitutable dependency.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Identifies the defensible layer: US SaaS incumbents face far less sovereignty risk than US IaaS, which is the layer European alternatives can actually serve.
insights.locator: European providers can supply IaaS and storage

insights.claim: Most European cloud alternatives are mostly marketing and do not offer services at the depth needed to be a real hyperscaler alternative, comparable to the early S3-clone era when vendors shipped a single server behind an S3 API.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Bearish read on European sovereign-cloud challengers as investments; the regulatory tailwind is not matched by product capability.
insights.quote: In Europe, most of the providers that provide an alternative, it's mostly marketing. They don't offer the kind of services to the level they should to be a real alternative.
insights.locator: Renato Losio was skeptical

insights.claim: About half of one European consultancy's client base — all of them European and adamant about keeping everything in Europe — is gradually migrating back on-premises, described as a clear observed trend rather than a one-off.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Repatriation as a sovereignty outcome, not just a cost one — a real if narrow headwind to hyperscaler European growth and a tailwind for on-prem hardware and private cloud.
insights.quote: All of our clients are within Europe and they're absolutely adamant on keeping everything within Europe. About half of our clients are actually gradually migrating back on-prem. It's absolutely a trend that I've seen.
insights.locator: Mark Silvester offered a concrete counter-signal

themes.theme: Hyperscaler agent arms race, gated by compliance

insights.claim: AI agents for cloud engineering were promoted from Innovators to Early Adopters this year, with hyperscalers shipping agent registries, DevOps agents, sandboxed execution environments — AWS and Microsoft DevOps agents, Google's GKE Agent Sandbox, Cloudflare dynamic workloads — in rapid succession.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Agent infrastructure is now a competitive product axis among all four major clouds — a category where feature parity arrives fast and differentiation shifts to governance.
insights.quote: I would say the agent infrastructure arms race basically going on. You see a lot of hyperscalers investing in products already.
insights.locator: AI Agents for Cloud Engineering

insights.claim: Enterprise agent adoption in regulated environments is gated by a specific coordination failure: individual teams racing ahead with AI without a shared foundation, duplicating each other's work, and colliding with security and compliance controls such as those introduced under DORA.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Regulatory frameworks like DORA are the real gating variable on enterprise agent revenue — vendors solving governance unlock spend faster than those adding capability.
insights.locator: Enterprise adoption, however, is gated by governance

insights.claim: A microservices-flavored agent architecture is emerging in which dedicated agents for coding, testing and CI are coordinated rather than replaced by a single all-powerful model, splitting the industry between teams betting on ever-larger frontier models and teams composing smaller purpose-built agents.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: The frontier-scale vs. composed-agents split is the key open architectural bet — which side wins determines whether value accrues to model labs or to orchestration tooling.
insights.locator: Agentic Infrastructure and Governance Automation

insights.claim: MCP's early adoption was suppressed specifically because agents inherited the permissions of whoever set them up, running roughshod over existing organizational IAM — a problem now addressed by a centralized auth plugin.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Names the concrete blocker that capped MCP enterprise deployment; its removal is the trigger to expect an enterprise MCP adoption step-up.
insights.quote: I have a perception of MCP coming in and just running roughshod over permissions and IAM that you have in your internal organization. And that inevitably has led to it not being adopted as much as it might have been.
insights.locator: Governance tooling is beginning to catch up

themes.theme: Platform teams pivot from builder to AI-native enabler

insights.claim: Platform engineering and the Model Context Protocol were both promoted to Early Majority this year because the debate has shifted from whether to adopt them to how best to operate them at scale.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Early Majority classification means budget is now recurring rather than experimental — the point where vendor revenue in these categories becomes durable.
insights.locator: Early Majority

insights.claim: Platform teams' non-AI work has entered a productive holding pattern — teams no longer debate how best to Terraform infrastructure — while the live debates have moved to data sovereignty, model hosting and access control around frontier models.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: Infrastructure-as-code tooling is a solved, low-growth market; the growth budget in platform teams has rotated to model hosting and access control.
insights.quote: teams are no longer debating how best to Terraform infrastructure, but rather data sovereignty, model hosting, and access control around frontier models
insights.locator: Matt Saunders described the discipline's non-AI work

insights.claim: Platform teams' main mandate with enterprise clients has become becoming AI-native enablers who avoid being a bottleneck, because when the central platform is not good enough teams build shadow platforms in completely different ways.
insights.speaker: Mark Silvester
insights.so_what: Shadow platform proliferation is the measurable failure signal for central platform investment — a diagnostic for whether a platform spend is working.
insights.quote: If the platform isn't good enough, then teams will want to do it themselves in a completely different way.
insights.locator: Platform Engineering

insights.claim: At KubeCon roughly 70% of a large audience considered platform engineering to be merely a rename of DevOps, evidence the discipline is still immature in perception even as its tooling consolidates.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: A perception gap that large means category messaging is still contested — expect continued vendor spend on category definition rather than pure feature competition.
insights.locator: At KubeCon, she found that around 70%

insights.claim: The platform engineer and developer roles are separating by abstraction layer, with developers moving to higher abstractions while platform engineers stay grounded in the engines, infrastructure and Kubernetes, and agentic developer portals emerging as a 'platform engineering 2.0' that should mature faster than IDPs did.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: Agentic developer portals are the next tooling wave to watch; the claim that it matures faster than IDPs implies a compressed adoption window for entrants.
insights.quote: Its time to move to platform engineering 2.0. Agentic developer portals are a new thing, and it's early days, like we've all seen with IDPs, but this time it'll mature faster.
insights.locator: She also drew a sharpening distinction

insights.claim: Limiting which tools are exposed through MCP has become a standard compliance checkpoint, making tool-surface minimization and least privilege the operational questions rather than whether MCP matters at all.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: Tool-surface governance is becoming a checkbox requirement — a concrete feature requirement for anyone selling MCP servers into enterprises.
insights.locator: Model Context Protocol (MCP)

themes.theme: Reliability forced back to the center

insights.claim: The most surprising trend of the year for one panelist had nothing to do with AI: how poor major cloud reliability was, including an AWS region offline for six months and US Virginia down for many hours last October with repercussions for half the internet.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Concrete outage evidence that undermines the implicit reliability premium in hyperscaler pricing and strengthens the multi-region and multi-cloud spend case.
insights.quote: If someone had told me one year ago we would have had a region of AWS off for six months, I could not have forecasted that. As well as US Virginia down for many hours last October, with quite some repercussions for half of the internet.
insights.locator: Cloud Reliability and Resilience

insights.claim: As new AI workloads strain cloud capacity, the fundamentals of reliability — multi-region design, operational readiness, resilience — matter more rather than less, and are not optional extras to bolt on after adopting the latest service.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Links AI capacity pressure directly to reliability degradation — a mechanism to watch as inference demand keeps climbing against fixed regional capacity.
insights.locator: The lesson is a familiar one that bears repeating

insights.claim: The big rocks of classic cloud waste have largely been addressed and what remains for deterministic cloud FinOps is incremental, with vendors extending mature tooling toward sustainability and green-computing reporting.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: Traditional cloud-cost tooling is a mature, low-growth market; growth requires the AI-spend pivot or a sustainability-reporting adjacency.
insights.locator: FinOps and Observability for Cloud

themes.theme: What the panel says is overrated

insights.claim: Agent washing — bolting agents onto products without adding value — echoes the earlier DevOps-veneer era, and in regulated settings such as health insurance fully autonomous decision-making is simply not permitted because a human or doctor must remain in the loop.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A regulatory ceiling on agent autonomy in insurance and healthcare caps the addressable automation in those verticals regardless of model capability.
insights.locator: A Note of Caution: What May Be Overrated

insights.claim: Several of the rapidly renamed and rebranded cloud AI managed services will not survive the next twelve months, as developers increasingly care about outcomes rather than which model runs behind the assistant.
insights.speaker: Renato Losio
insights.so_what: A dated, falsifiable prediction of service consolidation — expect hyperscaler AI service SKU rationalization within a year.
insights.locator: Over-proliferation of managed AI services

insights.claim: The narrative that AI will replace junior or senior engineers is fading, along with the more radical multi-year predictions of a completely transformed world.
insights.speaker: Matt Saunders
insights.so_what: A sentiment reversal from a practitioner panel — relevant to positioning against the AI-displaces-developers thesis in dev-tools and staffing.
insights.locator: Death-of-the-engineer predictions

insights.claim: Teams should stay conscious of the deeper problems — agentic meshes and harnesses — rather than being drawn to fancy portals and surface features, while keeping humans in the loop.
insights.speaker: Shweta Vohra
insights.so_what: A due-diligence filter: prefer vendors solving mesh/harness plumbing over those selling agent UI surfaces.
insights.locator: Fully autonomous agents in the enterprise

insights.claim: The teams best positioned for the next twelve months will be those that pair AI-enabled execution with platform governance and honest measurement, turning enthusiasm into durable value rather than accumulated cost and complexity.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: The report's synthesis: measurement and governance, not model access, is the differentiator to underwrite in enterprise AI execution.
insights.locator: Conclusion
